submission.natural_language_explanation: L4/N2176- is a retrospective phrase-onset detector read out through GELU's negative lobe: its pre-activation is raised to roughly -1.0 or higher on a token that follows a clause boundary or connective (a comma, period, newline, colon, or a word such as 'and', 'but', 'or', 'with', 'as', 'in', 'is'), and driven down to roughly -2.5 or below on the predictable continuation inside a phrase that a determiner, possessive or demonstrative has just opened ('the first', 'this time', 'the dog'). Since the pole reports |GELU(pre-activation)|, it sits at its 0.170 ceiling where that raise crosses the GELU trough (', a', '. This', '\nThe', 'but first', 'with time') and reads near zero both on the strongest onsets (pre above about -0.1) and on those phrase-internal continuations, so any ordinary text of more than a dozen tokens almost always contains a trough-band token and pins the pole at its ceiling while short determiner-locked fragments stay inactive.

The archive had been closed for nine years when the new curator arrived, and nothing about the building suggested that it held anything worth keeping. The shelves ran from floor to ceiling along three walls, thick with dust, and the boxes stacked against the radiator had never been catalogued at all. For the first two months she worked alone, opening one crate each morning and writing down whatever she found, and most of it was ordinary: ledgers from a shipping office, letters between distant cousins, a bundle of receipts from a hardware store that had burned down before the war. The work was slow and the room was cold, and there were afternoons when she carried a single box to the window and went through it twice because the handwriting was so small.

In the fourth week she found a folder of photographs, and behind the photographs a single page of handwriting that did not match anything else in the crate. The letters were careful and narrow, and the page listed dates, month after month, in a column down the right hand side. Some of those dates fell in years the town had no surviving records for at all. She photographed the page, typed the dates into a spreadsheet, and sent the file to a colleague who studied local history at the university. He replied within the hour, and his reply changed the shape of the whole project: the dates matched a set of harbour ledgers that everyone had assumed were lost in the fire, and if those ledgers existed, the harbour would sit at the centre of a trade route that nobody had thought to trace.

She went back to the shelves the same afternoon with a notebook and a lamp, and this time she read the label on every crate in the room. Two of them were marked with a colour she had never seen before, a faded orange that the archivist had not mentioned in any of her notes, and inside the first of those two crates was a bundle of letters tied with string. The handwriting on the topmost envelope matched the page exactly.
